matched_finding.subcategory: Fixed discussion items eliminate natural variation in misinformation exposure
matched_finding.description: The authors state that 'each pair will discuss the same set of four critical details during the collaborative recall phase.' While this ensures standardization, it eliminates natural variation in which details are discussed and potentially creates demand characteristics if participants notice that the discussion is structured. More importantly, it means that all participants receive misinformation on exactly the same four items, which may not generalize to real-world witness discussions where the topics of discussion vary. The counterbalancing of discussed vs. non-discussed items is mentioned but not fully described — it is unclear whether the assignment of which four of the eight critical details are discussed is counterbalanced across pairs.
matched_finding.quote: In order to ensure sufficient discussion, each pair will discuss the same set of four critical details during the collaborative recall phase. For example, all pairs will talk about Eric's cap color and his company logo.

matched_finding.subcategory: Contradiction in scoring of discussed items
matched_finding.description: The Analysis Plan contains two contradictory statements about how discussed items will be scored. First, it describes a nuanced approach where only partner answers that are inconsistent with the participant's version are classified as misleading (including the example that if a partner guesses correctly, it is not classified as misleading). Then, immediately after, it states 'we will categorize all discussed items as having contained misinformation, as the collaborative recall procedure is designed to expose participants to their partner's differing version of events.' These two approaches are contradictory: the first is item-level and contingent on actual partner responses, while the second treats all discussed items as misinformation-containing regardless of what the partner actually said.
matched_finding.quote: However, if the partner provided an answer consistent with what the participant had seen, that is, 'white mug'... the situation will not be classified as misleading... In addition, while scoring the individual memory test accuracy on the discussed questions (items containing misleading information), we will categorize all discussed items as having contained misinformation

matched_finding.subcategory: Inappropriate dismissal of normative influence without empirical justification
matched_finding.description: The authors claim that 'normative impact explanation of the memory conformity effect is completely ruled out in this study: participants work on their own and do not compare their answers with anybody, therefore there is no cost of disagreeing.' This dismissal is theoretically problematic. Normative influence can operate through anticipated social evaluation and internalized social norms even in the absence of direct observation — participants may still be motivated to agree with their partner's earlier statements to maintain social harmony or avoid appearing to contradict someone they interacted with. Research on social influence consistently shows that normative pressures persist even when responses are made privately. Ruling out normative influence entirely on the basis of private responding is an overclaim that is not empirically justified within this study.
matched_finding.quote: Given the fact that the individual memory test does not include any element of direct interpersonal pressure, we assumed that the normative impact explanation of the memory conformity effect is completely ruled out in this study: participants work on their own and do not compare their answers with anybody, therefore there is no cost of disagreeing.

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Open-ended→forced-choice changes baseline conformity rate and scoring categories — must know format matters
ground_truth.original_snippet: In the present research, the individual memory test will be in the form of open-ended questions.
ground_truth.modified_snippet: In the present research, the individual memory test will also use the two-alternative forced-choice format.
ground_truth.description: Changed from open-ended to forced-choice — inflates conformity rates (50% guessing baseline vs much lower); scoring categories (correct, misinformation, other) don't make sense with forced-choice

matched_finding.subcategory: Inconsistency between stated and planned measurement format
matched_finding.description: The authors state in the Analysis Plan that 'the individual memory test will also use the two-alternative forced-choice format,' but earlier in the Methods section they describe the individual memory test as containing '20 open-ended questions.' These are fundamentally different response formats with different psychometric properties, different susceptibility to guessing, and different scoring procedures. This internal contradiction makes it impossible to determine what the actual planned measurement format is. The power analysis was conducted based on effect sizes from forced-choice studies (Ito et al., 2019; Kękuś et al., 2020), which used forced-choice formats, so if open-ended questions are used, the power analysis is based on an inappropriate benchmark. If forced-choice is used, the description in the Materials/Procedure section is incorrect.
matched_finding.quote: The test will contain 20 open-ended questions... In the present research, the individual memory test will also use the two-alternative forced-choice format.

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Co-witness exposure exclusion removed — must know non-exposed participants dilute the effect
ground_truth.original_snippet: In addition, participants who are not exposed to co-witness details at all (that is, the participants who did not hear any potentially misleading information from the partner) will be excluded from the analyses.
ground_truth.description: Removed exclusion of non-exposed participants — including those who received zero misinformation dilutes the conformity effect and biases against finding both the basic effect and intervention benefit
